Berth reconstruction for larger cranes is the practical constraint on handling bigger vessels, and ports that defer it lose services to neighbours; the $84.6m for 1,333 feet is a useful per-foot benchmark for berth capex. The Spilman Island permitting spend converts a paper expansion into a real option with a defined regulatory pathway. Watch whether the Northside expansion reaches a formal final investment decision, since that is the trigger for material new Gulf container capacity.

headline: PJM market monitor: data centers drove $6.3B of the $16.4B latest capacity auction cost, and $29.4B over four auctions
players: Monitoring Analytics, PJM's independent market monitor, reported that data centers drove $6.3 billion of the $16.4 billion in charges from the most recent capacity auction (38%), and $29.4 billion of $63.6 billion across the last four auctions (46%). President Joseph Bowring argued data centers should either secure their own generation contracts or be served through dedicated 15-year capacity auctions, saying PJM 'is continuing to act like it's business as usual' and that failing to separate large loads 'imposes costs on other customers.'
why_it_matters: Quantifying the cost shift at 46% of four-auction capacity charges is the empirical basis regulators will use to justify separate large-load rate structures across PJM states. If dedicated 15-year data center auctions happen, they would create a distinct, long-dated capacity revenue stream that could be contracted against — attractive for new-build financing but a significant repricing for load. It also raises political risk for merchant asset owners who benefit from the current socialized structure. Watch state commissions and the FERC response, and whether hyperscalers preempt by self-supplying.

headline: MISO to build a dedicated expedited study process and non-firm transmission service for large loads
players: RTO Insider reported on July 20, 2026 that MISO will create a new expedited study process for large loads conducted outside its regular interconnection queue, together with a non-firm transmission service option for large loads, as its existing queue fast lane winds down. The design responds to FERC's show cause proceeding in Docket EL26-70.
why_it_matters: MISO is the second RTO after SPP to design a curtailable, fast-track path for large loads, confirming that non-firm service is becoming the standard bridge product across US markets. That accelerates time-to-power for data centers in the Midwest and Delta regions, which have land, water and gas advantages but slower queues than ERCOT. It simultaneously creates demand for firming generation and storage co-located with those loads, since non-firm service is not bankable on its own. Watch MISO's FERC filing and whether it adopts SPP's seven-year CHILLS tenor.

headline: Partners Group closes fourth direct infrastructure programme at more than $15bn
players: Partners Group held a final close on more than $15bn for its fourth direct infrastructure programme, focused on building next-generation energy, utility and other infrastructure platforms with an emphasis on mid-market opportunities. Investors included public and corporate pension plans, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments, foundations, GPs, consultants and banks across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia Pacific. Deployment to date was not disclosed.
why_it_matters: A near 50/50 split between commingled fund and separate accounts is the defining structural shift in infrastructure fundraising and explains how headline programme sizes keep growing while pension commitment counts fall. Managers that can offer bespoke mandates alongside a flagship are capturing a disproportionate share of the shrinking LP cheque pool, which compounds competitive advantage on large single-asset deals. At $15bn of direct equity aimed substantially at digital and power, this adds real bid pressure to data centre platforms and contracted generation at a time when auction processes are already crowded. Watch whether other large managers formalise the same dual-vehicle structure in their 2026-27 raises.

headline: EQT secures $9.4bn in three months for AI infrastructure fund anchored on EdgeConneX
players: Infrastructure Investor reported on July 20, 2026 that EQT had secured $9.4 billion for an AI-focused infrastructure fund. The same briefing noted GIP had a record busy year and that IFM is targeting $2 billion for a value-add strategy. EQT had earlier been reported on June 8, 2026 to be targeting €21 billion for an upcoming fund.
why_it_matters: Dedicated AI infrastructure vehicles are now a distinct fundraising category rather than a sleeve inside flagship funds, which tells you LPs are willing to take concentrated thematic exposure at scale. That concentration of capital into data centres, power for compute and adjacent fibre and grid assets is the main driver of entry multiples in digital infrastructure and is why co-located generation rights command a premium. The risk is vintage concentration: a large cohort of AI-dedicated capital raised in 2026 must deploy into the same finite set of powered sites. Watch deployment pace versus the pace at which large-load interconnection actually clears in PJM, ERCOT and SPP.

headline: Sandvik posts record Q2 with 17% organic order growth and adjusted EBITA margin of 22.6%
players: Sandvik reported second quarter 2026 order intake of SEK 37,799 million, up 17% organically, and revenues of SEK 36,752 million, up 23% organically at fixed exchange rates. Adjusted EBITA reached SEK 8,306 million against SEK 5,629 million a year earlier, lifting the adjusted EBITA margin to 22.6% from 19.0%. Adjusted diluted earnings per share were SEK 4.59. Free operating cash flow fell to SEK 3,590 million from SEK 5,090 million. The report was signed by CEO Stefan Widing on July 17, 2026.
why_it_matters: A 360 basis point margin expansion in a single year on mining and rock solutions demand is a strong read on the underlying commodity capex cycle, and it flows directly into the earnings power of mining services and consumables platforms that infra and PE buyers target. The divergence between record profitability and falling free operating cash flow is the flag — working capital is absorbing the growth, which is normal at cycle inflections but raises the cash conversion risk in any leveraged acquisition of a similar business. Ground support and consumables are the annuity portion of this exposure and should be valued above equipment. Watch whether order intake growth of 17% sustains into the second half or whether this proves to be a restocking peak.

headline: Epiroc Q2 orders up 13% with equipment orders up 30% organically and 20.1% adjusted operating margin
players: Epiroc reported second quarter 2026 orders received of SEK 17,305 million, up 13% and 13% organically, against SEK 15,276 million a year earlier, with large orders above SEK 150 million totalling SEK 720 million versus SEK 230 million. Revenues rose 10% to SEK 16,702 million, up 11% organically with a 1% currency headwind. Operating margin reached 19.9% from 18.7% and adjusted operating margin 20.1% from 19.7%. Equipment orders surged 30% organically, driven by copper and gold prices, with exploration strongest and service demand described as solid. The report was published July 17, 2026.
why_it_matters: Equipment orders up 30% organically while total orders grew 13% means the growth is concentrated in capital goods rather than aftermarket — a classic late-cycle signature that carries more downside when metals prices turn. The aftermarket and service book is the part that matters for infra-style underwriting because it is recurring and margin-accretive, and it grew only modestly. Exploration strength is the leading indicator: it precedes mine development by years and supports a multi-year demand runway for ground support, consumables and underground contracting. Watch copper and gold price durability and whether service revenue growth catches up to equipment, which is what would justify paying infrastructure multiples for mining services platforms.

headline: Port of Oakland June loaded container volume up 10.3% on import and agricultural export growth
players: The Port of Oakland handled 181,356 TEU in June 2026, up 7.7% year on year, with loaded containers up 10.3% to 143,254 TEU. Full imports rose 11.1% to 78,114 TEU and full exports rose 9.3% to 65,140 TEU, while empties fell 1.1%. Vessel calls rose to 81 from 77. First-half 2026 volume was 1,114,665 TEU, down 2.5%, though loaded cargo grew 0.3%. Acting Maritime Director Jason Garben described June as a solid month with growth in both imports and exports.
why_it_matters: Oakland is the one major US West Coast gateway where loaded exports are close to half of loaded volume, so it is a genuinely balanced trade port and a better read on real demand than Los Angeles or Long Beach. Export growth of 9.3% signals Californian agricultural shipments are moving despite freight rate and tariff noise — relevant for anyone underwriting refrigerated warehousing, cold storage or agricultural transload assets in the Central Valley corridor. The first-half decline of 2.5% against a positive June shows the recovery is recent and thin. Watch whether the export momentum holds through harvest season, since agricultural volumes are what differentiate Oakland's throughput risk profile.

headline: ECP VI heads for about $8bn close after LPs approve hard-cap increase to $7.8bn
players: Energy Capital Partners had raised $7 billion for ECP VI as of July 17, 2026, against an original $5 billion target, and LPs approved lifting the hard cap from $7.5 billion to $7.8 billion. The fund invests in energy infrastructure across North America and Europe, spanning energy transition, renewables, solar, wind, storage and natural gas. Dakota reported the fund at $4.8 billion in May 2026 approaching a summer final close.
why_it_matters: Going from a $5bn target to a $7.8bn revised hard cap, with LPs voting to let it happen, is about as strong a demand signal as the energy infrastructure fundraising market produces. The mandate flexibility across gas and renewables is exactly what LPs now want, given that the highest-returning assets are dispatchable gas serving data centre load rather than pure renewables. ECP is simultaneously deploying at scale, it is the co-bidder with KKR on the £5.75bn DCC Energy take-private, so the capital has a home. Watch the final close number and how much co-investment sits alongside, since ECP's recent deals have all required syndication well beyond fund capacity.

headline: Ratepayer advocates from five states attack FERC's show cause order for failing to remedy data center cost shifts
players: On July 17, 2026 state ratepayer advocates from Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Ohio and Pennsylvania filed responses in Docket EL26-67 arguing FERC's June show cause order to PJM failed to address cost allocation for network upgrades driven by data centers. They argued it is 'arbitrary and capricious and contrary to the Federal Power Act' for the Commission to conclude it has a duty to address the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers while failing to remedy the actual cost shifts.
why_it_matters: Cost allocation is the open question that determines whether transmission network upgrade costs for data centers land on load or on the interconnecting customer, and it is worth billions across PJM alone. If advocates prevail, large loads absorb far more of the upgrade cost, which raises the total cost of ownership for data center campuses and improves the position of utilities and existing ratepayers. If FERC leaves it alone, the socialised-cost model persists and supports faster data center buildout but invites state legislative retaliation. Watch FERC's order on the RTO responses and whether it opens a separate cost allocation proceeding.

headline: BofA: US needs 230+ GW of new capacity by 2030 against ~93 GW planned, leaving a 100-GW-plus shortfall
players: Bank of America analysis reported July 17, 2026 estimates the US needs more than 230 GW of new generating capacity through 2030 while utilities plan only about 93 GW, a shortfall exceeding 100 GW. Data centers alone are expected to add roughly 125 GW of electric demand, driving overall electricity demand growth of 4.1% compounded from 2026 to 2030. More than 7.5 GW of data center projects with on-site generation are already under construction, with another 60 GW-plus in pre-construction. Large gas turbines are described as largely sold out through 2030, pushing adoption toward reciprocating engines from Caterpillar, INNIO, Rolls-Royce and Wärtsilä; utilities are extending coal operations in Maryland, Wisconsin, Indiana, Utah, Kansas, Nebraska and Mississippi.
why_it_matters: A 100-GW planning gap is the core scarcity thesis in one number, and it explains why behind-the-meter generation is scaling from 7.5 GW under construction to a 60 GW-plus pre-construction pipeline. For investors, the shortfall supports elevated merchant spark spreads, capacity values and the strategic worth of any asset with firm capacity rights. It also flags coal life-extension as an unexpected near-term value pocket in specific states. Watch reciprocating-engine order books as the real-time indicator of how much load is giving up on the grid.

headline: Avangrid promotes Ryan Shields to SVP Finance & Corporate Development and Teresa Bradford to SVP & Controller
players: Avangrid announced that Ryan Shields, previously SVP of Corporate Development, was promoted to Senior Vice President, Finance & Corporate Development, and Teresa Bradford, previously VP, Strategic Initiatives Controller, was promoted to Senior Vice President & Controller, both effective July 15, 2026 and reporting directly to the CEO. Shields will oversee treasury, corporate development, sustainability, financial strategy, capital allocation and long-term growth initiatives. The company described the change as a return to Avangrid's previous organizational model.
why_it_matters: Consolidating treasury and corporate development under one SVP reporting to the CEO is the structure a company adopts when transaction activity and capital allocation are being run as a single workstream. For anyone tracking Iberdrola's North American portfolio rotation, the person who now owns both the balance sheet and M&A is the relevant counterparty. The release explicitly references continuity on key strategic projects and transactions, which is consistent with an active pipeline but discloses nothing about specific assets. No renewables divestiture or ArcLight transaction was announced by Avangrid or Iberdrola in the review period on the channels checked; treat this as an organisational signal only.

headline: FERC directs NERC to develop reliability standards for large computational loads by end of 2026
players: At its July 16, 2026 open meeting FERC directed NERC to submit reliability standards addressing the most essential reliability challenges from computational large loads by December 31, 2026, and to revise its registry rules. At the same meeting FERC ordered CAISO and SPP to file a joint report on seams coordination with a 30-day public comment period, and approved streamlined NEPA procedures and expanded categorical exclusions for minor hydropower actions.
why_it_matters: Mandatory reliability standards for data center loads would impose ride-through, voltage and frequency performance obligations on the load side for the first time, converting what is now contractual into enforceable and auditable. That creates real capex requirements at data centers — power electronics, UPS configuration, controls — and a compliance risk that acquirers will need to diligence. The context is the July 23, 2026 Virginia line fault that dropped roughly 3 GW of data center load, which is precisely the behaviour NERC is being told to standardise. Watch the NERC standards development timeline and the registry rule changes that determine which entities are subject.

headline: Fitch cuts Brightline Florida senior Opco bonds to CC as reserves are substantially depleted after July 1 payments
players: Fitch downgraded Brightline Florida's $2.219bn senior Opco bonds to CC from CCC, citing a very high probability that both issuers will be unable to fully fund the next debt service payments due on or before January 1, 2027. Fitch noted reserve accounts for both bond sets were substantially depleted to meet the July 1 payments. Concurrently bondholders agreed to move the AAFOH interest payment from July 15 to July 24 and the commuter mandatory redemption from July 14 to July 23, the 13th amended commuter indenture and fourth AAFOH supplement.
why_it_matters: A CC rating from Fitch is an explicit statement that default is probable rather than possible, and it removes the ratings cover some institutional holders need to keep the paper. Reserve depletion is the operative fact: the July 1 payments were made out of the last liquidity buffer, not out of operations, so the structure now has no cushion for the next cycle. Senior Opco holders and Assured Guaranty as insurer are directly affected, and the subordinate AAFOH and commuter tranches sit behind an issuer that has just spent its reserves. January 1, 2027 is the hard date Fitch has drawn a line at. Between now and then, the question is whether an equity raise or new-money financing lands before the next indenture roll expires.

headline: Blackstone launches dedicated APAC infrastructure platform, hires KKR's Ami Momaya to lead India
players: Blackstone launched a dedicated Asia Pacific infrastructure platform and hired Ami Momaya as Managing Director and Head of Infrastructure for India, its first dedicated infrastructure hire in the region. Momaya joins from KKR India, having previously worked at the National Infrastructure Investment Fund and spent 17 years at Morgan Stanley Investment Management. Blackstone's infrastructure business runs about $84bn of AUM with a long-term buy-and-hold approach across energy, transportation, digital, and water and waste, and already owns APAC data centre platform AirTrunk.
why_it_matters: Blackstone has been a large owner of Asian infrastructure through AirTrunk without a dedicated regional infrastructure team, so this formalises origination in the one geography where it has been a follower rather than a leader. India is the specific target, and the hire's NIIF background matters because Indian infrastructure deal flow runs through government-adjacent channels and InvIT structures. The strategic question for competitors is pricing, Blackstone entering Indian roads, transmission and digital infrastructure at scale would compress returns in a market that has been comfortably clubby. Watch the first control transaction and whether Blackstone raises a dedicated APAC infrastructure fund or deploys from the global pool.

headline: Port of Long Beach June volume up 10.6% to 779,331 TEU as retailers front-load ahead of August tariffs
players: The Port of Long Beach moved 779,331 TEU in June 2026, up 10.6% year on year and its third-busiest June. Loaded imports rose 11% to 387,025 TEU, loaded exports fell 1.3% to 86,446 TEU and empties rose 14.1% to 305,860 TEU. First-half volume reached 4.83 million TEU, up 1.7%. Retailers accelerated shipments ahead of tariff increases expected in August, with the National Retail Federation forecasting US container imports could hit a record 2.47 million TEU in July.
why_it_matters: The same pattern as Los Angeles — double-digit June against 1.7% first-half growth — confirms the West Coast complex is running on borrowed volume rather than underlying demand. Declining loaded exports alongside surging empties means the trade imbalance is widening, which raises repositioning costs for carriers and reduces backhaul revenue for drayage and rail intermodal operators serving the gateway. A record 2.47 million TEU national July followed by an expected August fall-off is a classic whipsaw that stresses terminal labour scheduling and chassis pools. Watch the NRF monthly forecast revisions and the size of the post-tariff air pocket, which is what will determine second-half terminal revenue.

headline: US rail traffic growth slows to 1.5% in week ending July 11 as carloads turn negative
players: AAR data for the week ending July 11, 2026 showed US traffic of 503,525 carloads and intermodal units, up 1.5% year on year. Carloads fell 0.4% to 223,040 while intermodal rose 3.0% to 280,485. Eight of ten carload categories gained, with metallic ores up 1,627 to 21,857 and nonmetallic minerals up 1,263 to 32,823, but coal fell 4,713 carloads to 53,527 and grain fell 1,197. Year-to-date US traffic through 27 weeks reached 13.65 million units, up 3.4%, with North American traffic of 18.79 million units up 2.9% and Mexican intermodal up 55.4% for the week.
why_it_matters: The deceleration from 7.2% in mid-June to 1.5% in mid-July, with carloads turning negative, is the first clear sign that the import pull-forward is running out and that second-half rail volumes will be weaker. That directly affects Class I revenue guidance and, downstream, the volume assumptions in short-line and transload underwriting. Mexican intermodal up 55% for the week is the standout — nearshoring volumes are growing off a small base at rates that justify capital into cross-border terminal and transload capacity. Coal down roughly 4,700 carloads a week in both June and July confirms the decline is structural, not weather. Watch August weekly prints for confirmation of the slowdown.

headline: Port of Los Angeles posts busiest June on record at 1,002,734 TEU, up 12% year over year
players: The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,002,734 TEU in June 2026, its busiest June in 118 years and only the third month ever above one million containers. Loaded imports rose 13% to 530,558 TEU, loaded exports were flat at 126,365 TEU and empties rose 17% to 345,811 TEU. First-half 2026 volume was 5,122,603 TEU, up 3%. Executive Director Gene Seroka said the results came without vessel backlogs or cargo delays as shippers advanced cargo ahead of trade policy changes.
why_it_matters: Record monthly throughput achieved with no congestion is the key operating datapoint — it means the gateway is absorbing peak volume within existing terminal, drayage and rail capacity, which caps the near-term case for new capacity investment on the San Pedro complex. The composition is less encouraging: imports and empties drove the gain while loaded exports were flat, so the volume is tariff-driven pull-forward rather than structural demand growth. Half-year growth of only 3% against a 12% June tells you the base is being borrowed from later months. Watch August and September volumes for the payback, and treat any terminal underwriting anchored to first-half run rates as optimistic.

headline: FTAI Infrastructure sets Q2 2026 results for August 5 after close, with call August 6
players: FTAI Infrastructure Inc. said it plans to announce second quarter 2026 financial results after the close of Nasdaq on Wednesday, August 5, 2026, with a management conference call on Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time.
why_it_matters: August 5 is the first scheduled disclosure point after both the Tidewater Logistics closing and the pending Long Ridge sale, so it is where management must update on Q3 closing timing and regulatory approval status for the $1.52bn MARA transaction. Expect the deleveraging bridge, specifically the $1.16bn of Long Ridge debt elimination and roughly $300m of corporate debt repayment, to be the number the market focuses on. Repauno Phase 2 remains guided to early 2027 commencement, and any slip there would be disclosed on this call. Segment EBITDA trajectory for Railroad and Jefferson Terminal will determine whether the post-Long Ridge business can carry the remaining capital structure.

headline: Lightpath signs 10-year second anchor tenant on eastern Pennsylvania AI-grade fibre build, lifting regional capacity ~30%
players: Lightpath secured a second infrastructure tenant, described as a leading multinational data centre developer and operator, on its 100% underground multi-conduit build in the Susquehanna region of eastern Pennsylvania under a 10-year anchor agreement. The tenant will use more than 60% of the combined eastern Pennsylvania system and adds another multi-gigawatt campus, increasing planned regional capacity by roughly 30%. Dollar terms undisclosed.
why_it_matters: This is the core economics of the multi-conduit model: the second tenant on an already-committed trench carries close to no incremental construction cost, so it converts almost entirely into margin and IRR uplift. A 10-year anchor term from an investment-grade-style data centre developer gives the cash flow a contracted, infrastructure-grade profile rather than telco churn risk. For MSIP it validates the strategy of underwriting builds on one anchor and treating subsequent tenants as free option value. Watch whether Lightpath discloses a third tenant on the same system and how much of the 30% capacity increase is pre-committed versus speculative.

headline: DOE court filing concedes $7.6B of clean energy grant cancellations were based on recipients' state political identity
players: In a July 15, 2026 court filing, the Department of Energy stated that its cancellation of 223 clean energy project grants worth $7.6 billion, noticed in October 2025, was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state and not on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor. All 223 cancelled grants were in states that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024. A judge had previously reversed DOE's cancellation of $82.1 million in clean energy grants as of June 12, 2026.
why_it_matters: An admission of arbitrary decision-making is close to a concession under the Administrative Procedure Act and materially raises the odds that cancelled awards are reinstated, which restores capital stack assumptions for the affected projects. More broadly it establishes that federal grant awards carry political-reversal risk that must be discounted in project financing, which pushes sponsors toward structures that do not depend on discretionary federal funding. Expect lenders to haircut or exclude uncommitted federal grants from base-case coverage ratios. Watch whether courts vacate the full set of 223 cancellations.

headline: Brightline West has raised about $5.5bn of a $21bn budget; completion target slips to late 2029
players: Brightline West has raised approximately $5.5bn against a $21bn total project cost for the 218-mile Las Vegas to Rancho Cucamonga corridor, leaving a reported $15.5bn gap, with a $6bn federal loan still awaiting approval. Director of public affairs Antonio Castelan said the project is advancing with contract execution. Named contractors include Atlas Technical Consultants and Las Vegas Paving on Nevada track, McCarthy Building Companies and Grimshaw Architects on the Las Vegas station, and HNTB and Whiting-Turner on the 200,000 sq ft Sloan maintenance facility.
why_it_matters: A $15.5bn shortfall against a $21bn budget is not a financing gap that closes with a single federal loan, and the slip from a pre-2028 Olympics target to late 2029 removes the deadline that had been driving urgency on the federal side. Contract execution continuing while financing lags means the sponsor is accruing commitments against uncommitted capital, which raises the cost of any later restructuring of the construction program. Equity is the binding constraint: prior reporting indicates bank lenders are prepared to sign but are conditioned on RRIF execution, and RRIF disbursement itself requires equity in place. For anyone holding Brightline West paper, the November bond maturity is the near-term event, not the RRIF decision.

headline: Holtec files for a Nasdaq IPO on its SMR-300 plans as the 800-MW Palisades restart nears completion
players: Holtec International filed an S-1 with the SEC to list on Nasdaq, per a July 15, 2026 report. Its 300-MW SMR-300 pressurized-water reactor is expected to receive regulatory approval in 2029 with first deployment in the early 2030s; Holtec claims a single-unit plant would need only 15 acres and three years to build. Separately, Holtec is restoring the 800-MW Palisades plant in Michigan — the first US effort to return a permanently shuttered reactor to service — supported by a $1.52 billion DOE Loan Programs Office award plus $400 million of DOE support for SMR-300 construction. As of July 10, 2026, Holtec had completed all major renovations with roughly 5,000 maintenance tasks outstanding, described as equivalent to a routine 34-day outage; the power sales contract begins next year. Holtec plans two SMRs at the Palisades site.
why_it_matters: An SMR developer seeking public equity while simultaneously completing the first US reactor restart gives the market a listed comparable that combines near-term operating cash flow with long-dated development optionality. A successful Palisades restart validates recommissioning as an asset class — the fastest and cheapest route to incremental firm carbon-free capacity — with obvious read-across to Three Mile Island and Duane Arnold. Note the timeline reality on new build: SMR-300 approval in 2029 and deployment in the early 2030s means SMRs cannot serve this decade's load growth. Watch the actual Palisades restart date and IPO pricing, which will set the market's discount rate for pre-revenue SMR pipelines.

headline: PJM's 2028/29 capacity auction clears at the $325/MW-day cap for a second time, with a 6.8-GW reserve shortfall
players: PJM's capacity auction for the 2028-2029 delivery year cleared at the $325/MW-day price cap and cost $16.4 billion, leaving the system 6.8 GW below its 20% installed reserve margin target. The auction procured only about 525 MW of new resources, including 208 MW of uprates to existing generation, versus 774 MW in the prior auction for 2027-2028, which cleared at the same cap with a 6.5 GW shortfall. Aurora Energy Research's Julia Hoos warned the current design 'doesn't work to bring online new capacity or stimulate demand response.'
why_it_matters: Two consecutive auctions at the cap with widening shortfalls confirm that PJM capacity revenue is now administratively bounded rather than market-cleared — the price signal is not producing supply. For owners of existing dispatchable generation in PJM, that means capacity revenue is capped but effectively assured, which supports asset values on a contracted-cashflow basis. For developers, it means capacity payments alone will not finance new build; bilateral large-load contracts are the route. Watch whether the proposed $555/MW-day backstop cap changes new-entry behavior or simply transfers more cost to load.

headline: GIP to acquire majority control of US community solar developer Summit Ridge Energy
players: Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock, agreed to acquire a majority and controlling interest in Summit Ridge Energy through its mid-market strategy; terms undisclosed. Summit Ridge operates more than 275 solar and energy storage facilities serving over 60,000 businesses, homes and municipalities across Midwest, Mid-Atlantic and New England markets, with more than 3GW of solar and storage operating and in development. Founder Steve Raeder remains CEO; close is subject to customary conditions and regulatory approvals.
why_it_matters: Community solar is a genuinely differentiated cash-flow profile, revenue comes from thousands of small subscribers at state-regulated tariffs rather than a single utility PPA, which diversifies counterparty risk but adds churn and billing complexity. GIP deploying its mid-market strategy rather than the flagship signals disciplined sizing on a segment where scale economics are real but individual projects are small. The entry comes as federal tax credit support sunsets, so the underwriting has to assume state programme durability rather than ITC continuation. Watch subscriber acquisition costs and state programme caps, which together determine whether the 3GW pipeline is financeable.

headline: Abu Dhabi's ePointZero completes $2.25bn all-cash purchase of Traverse Midstream at 11.3x EBITDA
players: ePointZero, a subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's 2PointZero Group, completed its $2.25 billion all-cash acquisition of Traverse Midstream Partners on July 14, 2026, buying a 35% stake in the Rover Pipeline and a 25% stake in the Ohio River System, both operated by Energy Transfer. The seller was The Energy & Minerals Group. The transaction implied roughly 11.3x EV/EBITDA against a historical midstream range of 10-12x, with the Alerian Midstream index trading near 10.8x forward as of late May 2026.
why_it_matters: An 11.3x print on non-operated minority interests in Appalachian long-haul pipe is a strong mark — buyers are paying above the listed sector for take-or-pay contracted cash flows with no operatorship and no growth capex obligation. That should widen the bid for other passive midstream stakes held by sponsors and pension funds. It also confirms sustained Gulf sovereign appetite for US gas infrastructure; UAE, Australian and Saudi capital is now setting the clearing price rather than domestic strategics. For sellers of minority pipeline interests, this is the comparable to cite. Watch whether contract roll dates on Rover create step-downs the multiple does not reflect.

headline: Bond Buyer: Brightline Florida distress raises contagion risk for Brightline West as $6bn RRIF loan stays pending
players: Bond Buyer reports Brightline West's $21bn capital plan comprises roughly $4bn bank debt, $4bn other debt, $4bn equity and $3bn grants, with $2.5bn of bonds swapped last year carrying a November maturity. The $6bn RRIF loan remains pending, with USDOT stating the Build America Bureau continues to work with the sponsor to obtain information required for the creditworthiness review. Both projects sit under Brightline Holdings LLC, backed by Fortress Investment Group; Assured Guaranty insures $1.13bn of the Florida senior bonds.
why_it_matters: The shared Fortress parent is the transmission mechanism: a Florida in-court process would put Brightline West's sponsor credibility in front of the same federal underwriters running the creditworthiness review. The November maturity on the $2.5bn of swapped Brightline West bonds is the nearest hard date and is independent of the RRIF timetable. Octus's Lucas Hammonds notes a huge funding hole remains even if the RRIF loan closes, so the $4bn equity component is the real gating item, not the federal debt. Allspring's Nick Venditti's comment that the story will be relived on the West Coast is the consensus buy-side read. Holders of the West paper should treat RRIF execution and equity commitment as sequential, not parallel, conditions.

headline: PJM 2028/2029 capacity auction clears at the $325/MW-day cap and falls 6,831 MW short of the reliability requirement
players: PJM's 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, announced July 14, 2026, cleared at $325/MW-day UCAP — the administratively set price cap negotiated with state governors and FERC — a 2.5% decrease from the prior year. It procured 138,318 MW through the BRA plus 10,864 MW from Fixed Resource Requirement regions for 149,182 MW total, at a cost of roughly $16.4 billion, with a 14.7% reserve margin. Cleared capacity fell 6,831 MW short of PJM's reliability requirement, the first time the entire RTO failed to meet the one-event-in-10-years standard.
why_it_matters: A capped, short auction is the clearest possible signal that PJM's price signal is no longer clearing supply and demand, which caps the upside on merchant generation revenues while leaving scarcity risk with load. For infrastructure owners this compresses the option value in PJM thermal and storage assets that were being underwritten on uncapped scarcity pricing, and pushes value toward bilateral contracts and out-of-market backstop procurement. It also strengthens the case for co-located and self-supplied generation, since grid capacity is demonstrably unavailable at the cap. Watch the backstop auction in late September and the 2029/30 BRA scheduled for December 9, 2026.

headline: Blackstone, Apollo and KKR to invest $5.34bn for 49% of Williams' behind-the-meter Power Innovation JV
players: Williams agreed a $5.34bn investment from Blackstone and partners Apollo and KKR for a 49% non-controlling equity interest in its Power Innovation joint venture, with Williams retaining 51% and operational control. The commitment comprises $4.4bn representing 49% of growth capex plus $0.9bn of additional consideration. The JV holds five behind-the-meter projects, Socrates, Apollo, Aquila, Socrates the Younger and Neo, part of Williams' 6GW-plus backlog; Williams holds buyout rights in years seven to fourteen at Blackstone's outstanding investment balance.
why_it_matters: This is structured equity dressed as a joint venture, the buyout right at outstanding investment balance caps the sponsors' upside and makes the return look like contracted yield plus a spread, which is why three large managers could share it without competing on multiple. For Williams the point is funding 49% of a capital-hungry backlog without consolidating debt or breaching a 3.5x-4.0x leverage target. Behind-the-meter generation contracted directly to data centre load is the highest-conviction cash-flow profile in US power right now, long-tenor, investment-grade counterparties, no merchant exposure. Watch whether this template, minority structured equity into midstream-sponsored power, becomes the standard route for funding the AI power build.

headline: Texas PUC advances a 12CP transmission cost allocation methodology to replace the long-standing 4CP regime
players: RTO Insider reported on July 12, 2026 that the Texas Public Utility Commission is moving forward through rulemaking with a 12 Coincident Peak transmission cost allocation methodology, expanding from the current four coincident peak mechanism to twelve monthly peaks.
why_it_matters: 4CP has for years driven the summer peak-shaving behaviour that underpins much of ERCOT's demand response and behind-the-meter generation economics, and moving to 12CP removes a large part of that arbitrage. Owners of load-side assets built to avoid 4CP charges — batteries, backup gen, curtailment programmes — face a direct revenue impairment. Conversely it spreads transmission cost recovery more evenly and reduces the incentive for concentrated summer peak avoidance, which is a modest positive for grid utilisation and for large flat loads like data centers. Watch the final rule and the effective date, which will set the transition period for existing 4CP-driven contracts.

headline: Carlyle sells power and AI infrastructure platform Copia Power to EQT Infrastructure VII after five-year hold
players: Carlyle agreed to sell Copia Power to EQT Infrastructure VII; the announcement did not disclose terms, though press coverage put the deal at about $2.6bn. Copia has taken 2.6GW of assets into operation or construction and holds a pipeline of over 30GW, comprising more than 25GW of solar and storage, 7GW of natural gas generation and 9GW of grid-connected data centres. Carlyle built the platform from inception in 2021, a five-year hold.
why_it_matters: This is a pure development-platform exit, the value is in interconnection positions, land control and permitting rather than operating cash flow, which is why the 30GW pipeline number carries the price. The inclusion of 7GW of gas and 9GW of grid-connected data centre capacity is what turns a solar developer into an AI-adjacent asset, and that reclassification is doing a lot of work in the valuation. A five-year build-to-exit on a ground-up platform is fast, and it validates the model of incubating developers inside infra funds rather than buying operating fleets. Watch whether EQT funds the pipeline out of Infrastructure VII or syndicates it, since 30GW is far beyond a single fund's capacity.

headline: MSIP to acquire majority stake in French waste and urban services platform Nicollin Environnement
players: MSIP agreed to acquire a majority stake in Nicollin Environnement, a French environmental services platform founded in 1945, with the Nicollin family retaining a minority position. Terms undisclosed; close expected Q4 2026 pending employee consultation and regulatory approvals. The business runs waste collection and sorting, urban street cleaning and water-related services across roughly 360 public contracts and 8,000 private clients, with about 4,800 employees and a 2,900-vehicle fleet. Paul Hastings and Natixis Partners advised MSIP; Clifford Chance and Rothschild & Co advised the family.
why_it_matters: Municipal waste and cleaning concessions underwrite like regulated infrastructure: multi-year public tenders, inflation indexation and high incumbent renewal rates, which is why sponsors keep paying up for the asset class. The explicit value-creation lever is fleet modernisation and decarbonisation across 2,900 vehicles, capex that can be recovered through contract renewals, plus buy-and-build in a fragmented French market. Control-with-continuity alongside a founding family is the standard French mid-market succession structure and typically prices below a competitive sponsor auction, which fits Chris Ortega's stated preference for bilateral mid-market situations. Watch the Q4 works-council process, renewal cadence on the 360 public contracts, and whether MSIP bolts on regional operators to build a national challenger to Veolia and Suez.

headline: Argo Infrastructure acquires eight-site C&I solar portfolio from NuGen, taking platform to 270MW
players: Argo Infrastructure Partners LP acquired an eight-site solar portfolio from NuGen Capital Management, LLC, comprising six sites in Massachusetts and two in New Jersey. Terms undisclosed. The acquisition expands Argo's commercial and industrial solar platform to 270MW across 196 sites. NuGen continues as a partner supporting asset performance post-close. Argo described the deal as its 21st investment since 2013.
why_it_matters: Distributed C&I solar in Massachusetts and New Jersey sits on top of two of the strongest incentive regimes in the US, with SMART and SREC-II programmes providing 10-20 year contracted revenue streams that are largely independent of merchant power prices. The value-creation lever is aggregation economics: at 196 sites and 270MW, Argo crosses the threshold where O&M contracting, insurance and tax equity recycling can be centralised rather than negotiated site by site. Retaining NuGen as operating partner is the standard structure that lets a financial owner buy the cash flows without building an in-house asset management team, and it keeps the developer aligned on future origination. Watch whether Argo converts the NuGen relationship into a programmatic development pipeline, and how interconnection queue timelines in ISO-NE and PJM affect the next tranche of build.

headline: Robotti & Company urges McDermott board to add oversubscription rights to $1.50 per share, 92% dilutive rights offering
players: Robotti & Company Advisors, holder of roughly 2% of McDermott's Class A ordinary shares, published a July 7 letter calling on the board to amend the rights offering to include an oversubscription privilege allocated pro rata ahead of the backstop parties. The offering contemplates up to 333.3 million new shares against 28.6 million outstanding at $1.50 per share, implying about $51m of pre-money equity value and roughly 92% dilution, backstopped by MFN Partners, Baupost Group, Mason Capital Management and First Pacific Advisors, two of which have board representation. Robotti argues the price massively undervalues a business with about $10bn of revenue, $489m of EBITDA, $17.6bn of backlog and a net cash balance sheet.
why_it_matters: This is a governance flashpoint in a post-restructuring capital structure where the backstop parties already sit on the board, and the absence of an oversubscription privilege means non-participating stock flows to insiders at $1.50. At roughly $51m implied pre-money equity against $489m of trailing EBITDA, the pricing gap Robotti identifies is large enough that minority holders have a real economic grievance, whatever the liquidity justification. The accredited-investor restriction compounds the problem by excluding some holders from participating at all. The operative deadline is the August 17, 2026 subscription expiry; if the board does not amend terms before then, minority positions are diluted at the announced price with no remedy short of litigation.

headline: Hydrostor says Willow Rock is nearing groundbreaking later this year with a signed project labor agreement and Hatch as EPC-M
players: Hydrostor said the 500 MW, eight-hour Willow Rock Energy Storage Center in Kern County, California is nearing groundbreaking and construction later this year, with a project labor agreement already signed and Hatch acting as EPC-M partner while Hydrostor contracts directly with vendors and suppliers. The company hosted contractor and supplier open houses in Rosamond and Bakersfield, reporting interest from more than 40 local vendors. It cited over $500m of direct and indirect benefits to Kern County and approximately $18m in annual property taxes, with around 40 permanent operating positions.
why_it_matters: Signing a project labor agreement and running local supply-chain outreach are the activities that immediately precede mobilisation, so this is a credible construction-start signal rather than a development update. The EPC-M structure, where Hatch manages but Hydrostor contracts directly, keeps procurement risk on the sponsor's balance sheet and makes the equity and debt package the real gating item. Willow Rock is the reference project for the DOE conditional commitment of up to $1.76bn and for the 50 MW California Community Power offtake, so a slip here reprices the whole platform. The next hard checkpoint is whether groundbreaking actually occurs in calendar 2026 and whether financial close is announced alongside it.

headline: Meridiam and Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust launch energy decarbonisation partnership with no upfront NHS capital
players: Meridiam and Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust launched a strategic partnership to design, finance and deliver energy system upgrades, with Dalkia Energy Services as technical partner. Investment size and contract length were not disclosed. Scope covers replacing fossil-fuel heating with low-carbon alternatives, building energy efficiency improvements and energy network modernisation, initially at St Thomas' Hospital in South London with potential expansion to other NHS Trusts and public bodies in southeast London. The partnership requires no upfront investment from the NHS.
why_it_matters: This is an energy performance contract structure where Meridiam funds the capex and recovers it from guaranteed energy savings and availability payments over a long concession, producing exactly the availability-based, public-counterparty cash flow that fits a core infrastructure mandate. The no-upfront-capital feature is the commercial unlock: NHS Trusts have net-zero mandates but no capital budget, so private-financed EPCs are effectively the only route, which gives first movers a strong origination position. The stated option to extend to other southeast London Trusts and public bodies is the real value here, turning a single-hospital contract into a platform with a repeatable template and shared delivery overhead. Watch disclosure of contract length and size, since the return depends entirely on tenor and savings-guarantee risk allocation, and whether the expansion pipeline converts.
companies: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust

headline: Lightpath to build AI-grade fibre to two new hyperscale campuses in Michigan and Wisconsin, each above 1GW
players: Lightpath will deliver triverse fibre infrastructure and multi-terabit capacity to two new hyperscale data centre campuses in Saline, Michigan and Port Washington, Wisconsin, each expected to exceed 1GW of capacity. The Saline build targets completion by end-2026 and Port Washington in Q2 2027, under a partnership with an anchor hyperscale customer. Contract term and dollar value not disclosed.
why_it_matters: Lightpath is following hyperscale campus development out of its legacy northeast metro footprint into new midwest markets, which is a meaningful change in the asset's geographic risk profile and addressable market. Triverse routing into gigawatt-scale campuses is a high-barrier product: the customer is buying physical diversity that cannot be replicated quickly, which supports long terms and pricing power. For MSIP the question is capital intensity, since anchor-led greenfield builds consume equity ahead of cash flow. Watch whether these builds are funded at the Lightpath level or require sponsor equity, and whether second tenants materialise on the same routes as they did in eastern Pennsylvania.

headline: Avangrid begins panel installation at 57 MWdc Oregon Trail Solar in Gilliam County, Oregon
players: Avangrid began installing over 100,000 panels at Oregon Trail Solar, a 57 MWdc / 41 MWac project in Gilliam County, Oregon, supporting 200 local union jobs during construction with completion expected in 2027. The project is expected to contribute $6m in combined payments in lieu of taxes and property taxes to Gilliam County over its life. Avangrid said it operates more than 2.5 GW of capacity in Oregon and has announced the adjacent Shutler Energy Storage project alongside the operating Pachwáywit Fields solar project. No offtaker or PPA counterparty was disclosed.
why_it_matters: Continued construction spend in Oregon indicates Iberdrola is still building out, not just harvesting, its US onshore renewables position, which is relevant to any thesis that the parent is a net seller of North American assets. The undisclosed offtake is the notable omission; without a named PPA counterparty it is hard to assess contracted cash flow quality for a potential portfolio sale. The clustering of Oregon Trail Solar, Shutler storage and Pachwáywit Fields creates a co-located package that would be more saleable as a bundle than as individual assets. Watch whether Avangrid discloses offtake or announces a portfolio process; nothing on either front surfaced in the review window.

headline: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank to take 15% of Morrison with $500m fund investment and $1.5bn raising pact
players: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank agreed to acquire a 15% stake in infrastructure manager Morrison, alongside an initial $500m investment split across Morrison Value Add II and The Morrison & Co Infrastructure Partnership. The arrangement includes a $1.5bn capital-raising agreement between the two firms. Valuation of the 15% stake was not disclosed.
why_it_matters: This is the now-familiar GP-stake-plus-distribution trade: the buyer gets economics on the management company, the manager gets a captive Japanese distribution channel and anchor capital. For Morrison, a $1.5bn raising commitment is transformational relative to its Australasian scale and effectively de-risks the next two fund vintages. Japanese institutional demand for hard assets is the structural driver here, and SMTB is buying access rather than just an income stream. Watch whether other mid-market infra managers follow with Japanese or Korean strategic minority sales, which would be the clearest sign that distribution, not performance, is the binding constraint on fundraising.

headline: USDOT awards $1.73bn in BUILD grants across 127 projects with $136.8m to ports and $87.7m to rail
players: USDOT announced $1.73 billion in BUILD grants on July 8, 2026 across 127 infrastructure projects in 52 states, territories and the District of Columbia. Road and bridge projects took $1.3 billion or 77% of the total, with $169.9 million to transit, $136.8 million to port infrastructure, $87.7 million to rail and $11 million to aviation. Named awards included $24.3 million to the Port of Corpus Christi Authority to modernise and lengthen track at its inland port facility and $8.5 million to Alaska Railroad Corp. to widen the Port of Seward freight dock by 300 feet. USDOT received nearly 1,200 eligible applications requesting over $14.5 billion.
why_it_matters: A 77% allocation to roads and bridges against 8% for ports and 5% for rail is a clear statement of federal priorities and should temper any underwriting that assumes discretionary grant funding will materially de-risk freight rail or terminal capex. The 12-to-1 oversubscription ratio means grant assumptions in project financings should be heavily discounted. For public-private freight projects, the practical implication is that sponsors must carry more of the capital stack themselves, which raises required returns and favours assets with contracted revenue rather than merchant volume. Watch the next RAISE and PIDP rounds for whether the port and rail share recovers.

headline: Quinbrook closes second UK renewables fund at £587m with 74% re-up rate
players: Quinbrook Infrastructure Partners held a final close of £587m for the Quinbrook Renewables Impact Fund, its second UK-focused renewables vehicle. Fundraising took roughly 18 months and the fund achieved a 74% re-up rate from investors in the predecessor strategy. Individual LP names were not disclosed.
why_it_matters: A 74% re-up rate is the substantive datapoint, it signals that UK value-add renewables has retained its LP base through a period when generalist energy transition fundraising has stalled. At £587m the fund is sized for build-and-operate solar, onshore wind and storage rather than trophy assets, which is where UK returns still price attractively given grid connection scarcity. The UK's capacity market and CfD framework provide a contracted revenue floor that supports leverage, with merchant upside on storage arbitrage. Watch deployment pace against grid connection dates, which remain the single largest execution risk in the UK market.

headline: Fervo says drilling rates are up 143% since its first Cape Station well, targeting $3,000/kW long term
players: Fervo said on July 8, 2026 that its third-generation well design has increased drilling rates 143% versus its first Cape Station well, with the Sawtooth 7 well drilled in 21 days to 19,448 feet measured depth including a 7,500-foot lateral. The company projects Cape Phase II will deliver power at approximately $5,500 per kilowatt of installed capacity, with a longer-term target of $3,000 per kilowatt.
why_it_matters: Published capex-per-kW targets give infra investors a concrete cost curve to underwrite instead of a technology story. At $5,500/kW today falling toward $3,000/kW, EGS starts to compete with new-build combined-cycle gas on an all-in basis while delivering 24/7 output that gas increasingly cannot get permitted or turbines for. Well-cost learning curves are the single biggest driver of geothermal IRR, so drilling-day reductions flow straight to equity returns. Watch whether the Phase II well set holds the 21-day pace at commercial scale — that is what converts the target into a bankable input.

headline: Pembina confirms Greenlight will supply dedicated gas-to-power for Meta's new Alberta data centre
players: Pembina Pipeline welcomed Meta's announcement of a new Alberta data centre project with the Government of Alberta, confirming that the Greenlight Electricity Centre partnership between Pembina, MSIP and Kineticor Asset Management will provide dedicated behind-the-meter gas-fired generation to the development. Pembina CEO Scott Burrows described dedicated, contracted gas-to-power infrastructure as a promising new growth platform. No incremental financial terms were disclosed.
why_it_matters: Naming the hyperscaler behind the tolling agreement materially de-risks the credit story on a C$4bn-plus greenfield: the counterparty quality is what determines whether this prices as contracted infrastructure or merchant Alberta power. Behind-the-meter, dedicated generation sidesteps AESO interconnection queues and transmission constraints, which is precisely why data centre developers are willing to sign long-term tolls at prices that support new-build gas. For MSIP this is the template it is likely to repeat: co-invest with a strategic midstream partner who supplies fuel and operates, take half the equity, and underwrite to a single-name long-term offtake. Watch for disclosure of toll tenor and any capacity expansion to the permitted 1,864MW as Meta's campus scales.

headline: UP and NS file first round of STB supplemental responses, offering to relinquish control of jointly owned terminal railroads
players: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern filed the first tranche of responses to the STB's May 28 information request on July 7, 2026, addressing jointly owned entities including the Terminal Railroad Association of St. Louis, Kansas City Terminal Railway and TTX Company. The carriers stated they will not control those entities post-merger and offered divestiture as an option. The filing reiterates a claim of $3.5 billion in annual shipper savings from single-line transcontinental service, with remaining responses due July 27 and completion targeted for mid-2027.
why_it_matters: Volunteering to give up control of TRRA, KCT and TTX is a meaningful concession and a template for what the STB will extract elsewhere — expect similar structural remedies on gateways and interchange. Terminal railroad and railcar-lessor assets that sit inside these joint ventures could come into play as divestiture candidates, which is a direct sourcing opportunity for infra funds. The $3.5bn shipper-savings figure is the applicants' own number and will be attacked in evidentiary rounds; do not underwrite it. Watch whether the STB treats the terminal concessions as sufficient or demands trackage rights grants that would compress the merged network's pricing power.

headline: IFM completes Atlas Arteria takeover, reaching 67.43% voting power in the toll road group
players: IFM Global Infrastructure Fund's bid vehicle Diamond Infraco 1 closed its off-market offer for Atlas Arteria on 7 July 2026 with 67.43% voting power, including acceptances settling up to 21 days later. The offer began with a bidder's statement on 27 April 2026, was initially rejected by the Atlas Arteria board on 6 May, and was raised in June before the board recommended it. Atlas Arteria owns 30.8% of the 2,424km APRR/AREA/A79/ADELAC French motorway network, 66.67% of the Chicago Skyway, a 100% economic interest in the Dulles Greenway and 100% of Germany's Warnow Tunnel.
why_it_matters: IFM has taken hard control of one of the last listed pure-play toll road vehicles, and at 67.43% it can drive distribution policy and refinancing without needing full compulsory acquisition. The prize is the APRR stake, inflation-linked French motorway tolls with concession tails into the 2030s, which is the closest thing to a bond substitute in the asset class. The Dulles Greenway remains the problem child, with tolls capped and traffic structurally below underwriting, and that is where IFM has room to restructure away from public-market scrutiny. Watch whether IFM moves to full ownership and delisting, and how it handles the Greenway's debt.

headline: InfraVia to acquire D-Marin, EMEA premium marina platform, from CVC Capital Partners VII
players: InfraVia Capital Partners agreed to acquire D-Marin from CVC Capital Partners VII. Terms undisclosed. D-Marin operates 28 premium marinas across nine countries including Turkey, Croatia, Greece, UAE, Spain, Italy, France, Malta and Albania, with over 14,300 berths of which more than 1,000 are dedicated superyacht berths, plus 12 professional boatyards servicing over 2,500 yachts annually. CVC acquired the business in 2020 and built it into the regional market leader.
why_it_matters: Marinas are concession or long-leasehold assets with multi-year berth contracts, high renewal rates and effectively fixed supply because coastal permitting is near-impossible, which gives them pricing power that reads more like a port than a leisure asset. The value-creation lever for InfraVia is continued consolidation of what it calls a fragmented market, plus yield management on superyacht berths where scarcity is most acute and rate growth has been strongest. Buying from a buyout sponsor that already executed the geographic roll-up means InfraVia is paying for a built platform, so returns depend on further M&A and boatyard services margin rather than the initial aggregation trade. Watch Turkish and Greek concession renewal terms, which concentrate a large share of berths, and whether InfraVia extends the platform into the western Mediterranean.

headline: Blackstone Energy Transition Partners to acquire Dresser Utility Solutions from First Reserve
players: Blackstone Energy Transition Partners agreed to acquire Dresser Utility Solutions from First Reserve; terms undisclosed. Founded in 1880 and headquartered in Houston, Dresser supplies metering and digital instrumentation, pressure and flow control, gas and water infrastructure repair products and utility software, employing roughly 850 people globally. Blackstone described it as the first investment from the latest vintage of its Energy Transition Partners private equity vehicle.
why_it_matters: This is an infrastructure-services asset rather than an asset-owning one: revenue is tied to utility maintenance and replacement capex, which is regulated rate-base spending and therefore non-discretionary through the cycle. That gives a defensive, high-recurring-revenue profile with pricing power on installed-base consumables, the sort of business that supports leverage without volume risk. As a first deal from a new fund vintage it signals Blackstone tilting energy transition capital toward picks-and-shovels rather than generation, where entry pricing has become punishing. Watch for bolt-ons in metering and leak detection, which is the obvious buy-and-build path.

headline: NERC's 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment flags New England and the Northwest at elevated risk in extreme scenarios
players: NERC's 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment projected all areas would have adequate resources under normal summer conditions but identified two US regions — New England and the Northwest — at elevated risk under extreme load scenarios. In a July 6, 2026 review, Grid Strategies argued the flagged regions would in fact hold between 5% and 93% more reserves than their target reserve margins once additional resources and mitigation measures were counted.
why_it_matters: Reliability assessments drive state procurement mandates, capacity market parameters and out-of-market emergency payments, so the framing matters commercially even where the underlying physics is contested. Elevated-risk designations support the case for new peaking capacity, storage and demand response contracts in New England and the Pacific Northwest. The Grid Strategies critique is a caution against underwriting scarcity revenues purely off NERC labels. Watch actual summer 2026 performance and whether ISO-NE's capacity reforms and the Maine transmission award change the 2027 assessment.

headline: MSIP takes 47.5% of Greenlight Electricity Centre, a 932MW Alberta gas plant tolled to a data centre customer
players: MSIP announced an investment in the Greenlight Electricity Centre in Sturgeon County, Alberta, taking a 47.5% interest alongside Pembina Pipeline (47.5%) and Kineticor Asset Management (5%). Pembina's 2 July FID disclosure put gross project cost at approximately $4bn (about $4.6bn including financing costs), funded roughly 60% debt and 40% equity, with about $310m of annual run-rate adjusted EBITDA net to Pembina and around 85% of costs secured under fixed-price agreements. The 932MW combined-cycle plant will consume roughly 150 MMcf/d of gas, run on Siemens Energy turbines, sell under a long-term tolling agreement to a data centre customer and enter service in H2 2030; Pembina is construction and operations manager. Santander advised MSIP on M&A and financing, with Kirkland & Ellis and Bennett Jones as legal counsel.
why_it_matters: This is MSIP's largest disclosed 2026 commitment and it is a development-stage, four-year-construction position rather than an operating asset, so the return is being earned for construction and completion risk with a fixed-price EPC wrap covering about 85% of cost. A long-term toll converts what would otherwise be merchant Alberta generation into contracted, availability-based cash flow, and the 60/40 capital structure implies roughly $1.8bn of equity split across the partners. Strategically it confirms MSIP is deploying into the power-for-AI trade through partnership structures with strategics rather than competing for stabilised data centre platforms at compressed yields. Watch the toll tenor and counterparty disclosure, EPC schedule against the Q3 2026 construction start, and whether the partners exercise the expansion to the permitted 1,864MW.

headline: Aecon-led consortium wins EPC for MSIP-backed Greenlight plant, with Aecon's share at C$1.7bn
players: Tecnicas Reunidas Alberta (TRA), a consortium in which Aecon is majority partner, was awarded the EPC contract for the Greenlight Electricity Centre, with Aecon's share valued at $1.7bn. Scope covers civil, piping, mechanical, structural, electrical and instrumentation works plus the gas metering station, switchyard and substation. The project is owned by Greenlight Electricity Centre Limited Partnership (Pembina 47.5%, MSIP 47.5%, Kineticor 5%), is 932MW in its initial phase and is permitted for expansion to 1,864MW; construction starts Q3 2026 with completion anticipated in 2030.
why_it_matters: The EPC award is the milestone that converts an announced FID into a real construction schedule, and the fixed-price structure is what allows the equity to be underwritten as infrastructure rather than development risk. The disclosure that the site is permitted to 1,864MW is the important detail: the second phase is effectively a free option on brownfield expansion at an already-permitted, already-interconnected site, which is where outsized returns in this trade will come from. Contractor capacity is now the binding constraint on new-build gas in North America, so locking a major EPC in mid-2026 for a 2030 in-service date is itself a competitive advantage. Watch for schedule slippage, turbine delivery slots, and whether the partners announce a phase-two toll before phase one completes.

headline: FERC denies ArcLight-backed developer's waiver to modify a $2B PJM fast-track gas plant, enforcing RRI rigidity
players: FERC on July 2, 2026 denied a waiver sought by Advanced Power Services, owned by ArcLight Capital Partners, to reduce the maximum output of its roughly $2 billion Chestnut Run gas plant in Carroll County, Ohio from 1.3 GW to 1.245 GW after equipment supply constraints forced a turbine substitution. The project entered PJM's Reliability Resource Initiative, an expedited process that initially covered 51 projects totalling roughly 9.3-11.8 GW and prohibits changes to project size and capacity rights. FERC found studies from the equipment change would introduce substantial delays to Transition Cycle #2 with ripple effects across PJM's study schedule.
why_it_matters: This establishes that fast-track interconnection comes with no flexibility, which is a material and underpriced risk for every RRI-track project in a market where turbine supply is the binding constraint. Developers must now lock equipment specifications before entering expedited queues or accept that supply chain slippage forfeits the queue position. It raises the value of secured turbine slots and of projects with equipment already ordered, and it should widen the valuation gap between shovel-ready and merely-permitted gas developments. Watch whether other RRI projects hit the same wall and whether PJM seeks tariff flexibility.

headline: PJM stakeholders advance registry-based backstop procurement but fail to agree on data center connect-and-manage
players: PJM stakeholders on July 2, 2026 approved a two-part reliability backstop procurement plan built on a registry-based subscription model developed by the Data Center Coalition and ten utilities including Dominion Energy, Duke Energy and Exelon. Utilities and load-serving entities can request PJM procure specific capacity through a one-time auction, with large loads billed for the cost and the procurement capped at $555/MW-day, preceded by a bilateral contracting phase. Stakeholders failed to reach consensus on a connect-and-manage framework for data centers, instead backing a large load registry giving state regulators data to set load-reduction priorities. PJM planned a board filing in July, a backstop auction in September 2026, and the 2029/30 capacity auction on December 9, 2026.
why_it_matters: The registry-and-subscription model makes large loads the direct payer for the capacity they cause to be built, which is the cleanest available answer to the cost-shift fight and the template most likely to spread to other RTOs. For generation developers it means a creditworthy, identifiable counterparty rather than socialised load, improving bankability of new-build. For data center sponsors it converts capacity cost from a pass-through into an explicit, budgetable line item at up to $555/MW-day. Watch the FERC filing and how many MW subscribe in September.

headline: Brightline Florida taps reserves to make July 1 payments on senior munis and corporate notes, buys two weeks on commuter bonds
players: Brightline drew on reserves to make scheduled July 1 payments on its $2.2bn senior municipal bonds and $1.1bn corporate notes. It negotiated a two-week extension on the $985m commuter bonds, moving the mandatory tender deadline from June 30 to July 14 and the grace period to July 15. A further payment on the $1.2bn AAF Operations Holdings subordinate municipal bonds was due July 15, with an option to trigger a third deferred interest election.
why_it_matters: Paying senior obligations out of reserves rather than cash flow is the moment the capital structure stopped being self-funding, and it is what drove Fitch's subsequent downgrade to CC. The differential treatment matters: senior munis and corporate notes got paid, commuter bonds got an extension, which tells you where the company and its advisers think the fulcrum sits. The third deferred-interest election on the AAFOH bonds is a contractual toggle, not a negotiation, so it buys time without requiring creditor consent. The company's own language about being compelled to pursue additional restructuring initiatives if it cannot obtain financing or extend maturities is the disclosure to anchor on.

headline: McDermott prices $550m of 10.5% Nordic bonds due 2031 alongside a $500m fully backstopped rights offering
players: McDermott priced $550m of senior bonds at a 10.5% coupon maturing July 2031, with application to be made for listing on Euronext Nordic ABM. Net proceeds will be applied toward cash collateralising letter of credit facilities, refinancing existing debt and general corporate purposes. The bond forms part of a broader refinancing alongside a $500m equity rights offering fully backstopped by major shareholders, with an ex-rights date of July 10, record date and special shareholder meeting on July 13, and a subscription period expiring August 17, 2026 at 4:59 p.m. ET. Expected closing is the third quarter of 2026; DNB Carnegie acted as global coordinator and joint bookrunner with Clarksons Securities as joint bookrunner.
why_it_matters: A 10.5% coupon on senior paper for a business generating $489m of trailing EBITDA with a net cash balance sheet is expensive, which tells you the market is still pricing McDermott on its post-restructuring history rather than current cash generation. The use of proceeds is revealing: cash collateralising LC facilities is a working-capital fix for a contractor that struggles to get uncollateralised bonding, and it is arguably the real purpose of the raise. Combining $550m of high-coupon debt with $500m of deeply dilutive equity means total consideration of over $1bn to solve a bonding and liquidity problem, which is the context for Robotti's objection. Q3 closing and the August 17 subscription expiry are the two dates that determine the final capital structure.
